newsitem.title: GERMANY: Krupp may have Thyssen stake - sources.
newsitem.headline: Krupp may have Thyssen stake - sources.

text.p: Steel and engineering firm Krupp AG may have already set aside a stake in rival Thyssen AG as a prelude to the takeover it still plans to achieve, banking sources said on Friday.
A German press report that Krupp had secured around 30 percent of Thyssen's capital with institutional investors was viewed as highly speculative, however.
"Whether it is 10 percent or 30 percent, that I cannot say," said a source close to the negotiations on Krupp's financing.

"But the whole reason this came up in the first place is that Thyssen had no protection for its shares. It (Thyssen) didn't even know who its shareholders were. So naturally Krupp will have taken some steps," the source said.

Germany's Handelsblatt newspaper reported on Friday that Krupp had parked some 30 percent of Thyssen with investors. It also said Krupp was still interested in taking control of its rival and had secured a 15 billion mark credit line from banks.
None of Krupp's Frankfurt-based banks -- Dresdner Bank AG, Deutsche Bank AG or Goldman Sachs -- was prepared to comment on details of the report.
A Dresdner Bank spokesman said: "We welcome Krupp's initiative to secure a merger in the steel sector. We think this is a positive move and are giving financial support."
Another source close to the deal stressed that Krupp was "totally committed" to getting some form of alliance with Thyssen, so much so that it would play things "completely by the book."
"The company is determined to bring about something new in Germany -- and it is very determined to stick to the rules," the source said.
That implied that Krupp would not build up a large stake in Thyssen itself but need not rule out its using other investors to hold shares on its behalf, the source added.
German share law demands that companies declare holdings of more than five percent in another corporation.
Krupp and Thyssen have now entered eight days of talks aimed at agreeing a merger, after Krupp temporarily suspended a hostile takeover bid that shocked the consensus-driven German industry.
Should no agreement result, Krupp has said it will reopen its takeover bid. Earlier this week, Krupp said it would offer 435 marks per share to Thyssen shareholders.
